72e44e5157f71fcf.body: Small business credit is growing at 26.2% this year and now makes up 23.1% of all business lending. Growth in micro and small business loans jumped by 23.8pp because government systems like UDYAM registration and GST data now let lenders check if tiny businesses are real and can pay back. Banks cannot reach thousands of small borrowers alone, so they lend through partners who find customers and do the checking.
72e44e5157f71fcf.implication: A bank should set up deals with NBFCs and fintech partners to lend money for small business loans, using the new government data to decide who gets credit.
chain: Government created UDYAM registration and GST records that prove small businesses exist and show their sales
These records let lenders check if tiny borrowers can repay, so lending to micro and small businesses jumped by 23.8pp
Banks need local partners to find and check thousands of small borrowers, so they should lend through NBFCs who do that work

274039457d240fc6.body: Banks are growing gold loans by 105.5% compared to last year, and this growth has continued for 12 straight periods. Gold prices jumped sharply between 2023 and 2026, so customers can now borrow much more money using the same gold jewelry or coins as security. Banks are winning customers from finance companies because they have local branches where staff can check the gold is real and store it safely, plus they charge lower interest rates.
274039457d240fc6.implication: Banks should open more gold loan counters in branches, train staff to test gold quickly, and advertise lower rates to pull customers away from finance companies while gold prices stay high.
chain: Gold prices rose sharply from 2023 to 2026, so the same gold jewelry is now worth more and customers can borrow bigger amounts against it
Banks have local branches with vaults and trained staff to verify and store gold safely, and they charge lower interest than finance companies, so customers are switching to banks
Banks should add more gold loan counters, speed up the testing process, and promote their lower rates to capture even more of this fast-growing market

22d3c3a94d23cee3.body: Small business lending is growing at 32.7% per year, and these tiny businesses now make up 23.1% of all MSME lending. Their growth rate jumped by 23.8pp recently, while bigger MSME borrowers are growing much slower—the gap is 11.8pp. Banks can now check if these small businesses can repay loans using government registration systems and GST records, which makes lending safer and faster.
22d3c3a94d23cee3.implication: Banks should invest in systems that connect to UDYAM registration and GST databases to quickly approve loans for small businesses, because these borrowers are growing fast and becoming easier to check.
chain: Small businesses are registering with the government and filing GST returns, creating digital records of their activity
Banks can now use these records to verify income and business health quickly, making it safer to lend to borrowers they couldn't check before
This opens up a fast-growing segment where demand is strong and competition is still light

6b8d3ec6057b841b.body: The government is paying big manufacturers to build new factories under a scheme, and those manufacturers need more parts from smaller suppliers. Lending to suppliers in basic metals grew 22.6% and 18.4%, chemicals grew 22.6% and 21.8% and 14.2% and 7.4%, and engineering grew 23.9% and 38.3%. These suppliers are safer to lend to because they have signed contracts with large established companies that guarantee payment.
6b8d3ec6057b841b.implication: Banks should lend to small and medium suppliers in metals, chemicals, and engineering who have confirmed orders from big manufacturers building new plants, because the contracts reduce the risk of non-payment.
chain: Government pays big manufacturers to build factories, so those manufacturers order more parts from smaller suppliers
Suppliers with confirmed orders from big companies are safer borrowers because the contracts guarantee they will get paid
Banks can lend more to these suppliers with lower risk, especially in metals, chemicals, and engineering where growth is fastest

cdde0ad92bf08131.body: Housing loans that count toward priority sector lending jumped 39.0% in one year because RBI raised the ceiling in October 2024. Banks did not reclassify actual new lending—they simply moved existing housing loans into the priority bucket under the new rule. This creates instant surplus PSL credits that banks can sell to other banks who fall short of their required priority sector targets.
cdde0ad92bf08131.implication: The bank should buy PSL credits from banks with surplus housing-loan classifications if it is short on priority targets, or sell credits if it now has excess after reclassifying its own housing book.
chain: RBI raised the housing loan ceiling that counts for priority sector in October 2024
Banks moved existing housing loans into the priority bucket without lending more money, creating a 39.0% jump in reported priority housing loans
Banks with surplus credits can now sell them to banks that need to meet their priority sector targets

3f7df2cc3058bd42.body: Old infrastructure lending is shrinking — some sectors fell -37.6% and -14.5% this year — while renewable energy sectors jumped 82.8% and 23.8%. Banks already have teams that know how to finance big, long-term projects like highways and power plants, and those same skills work for solar, wind, and green hydrogen projects.
3f7df2cc3058bd42.implication: The bank should move project finance teams from old infrastructure to renewable energy, because government targets mean these new projects now need the same kind of big, long-term financing that old infrastructure used to get.
chain: Old infrastructure projects are finishing and paying back loans faster than new ones are starting, so lending in those sectors is falling
Renewable energy projects are growing fast because of government targets, and they need the same kind of long-term project financing
Banks can use their existing project finance skills and teams to lend to solar, wind, and green hydrogen instead of waiting for old infrastructure to recover

b263abfde31bb531.body: Services sector lending is growing at 20.4% per year and now makes up 28.3% of all bank credit. Banks are lending more through NBFCs that serve services companies — this channel grew 19.7% and is getting stronger. Three services sub-sectors are growing extremely fast: one at 54.9%, another at 41.0%, and a third at 33.7% per year.
b263abfde31bb531.implication: Banks should build or expand partnerships with NBFCs that lend to fast-growing services sub-sectors, especially the three racing ahead at 54.9%, 41.0%, and 33.7%, to capture this 20.4% growth wave without taking all the direct risk.
chain: Services companies need more credit and the sector is growing at 20.4% yearly, now 28.3% of all bank loans
Banks are using NBFCs as a safer way to reach these borrowers, and that NBFC channel just grew 19.7%
Three specific services areas are exploding at 54.9%, 41.0%, and 33.7%, so banks lending through NBFCs to those pockets can grow fast while sharing the risk

a6c393217b7740b0.body: India has 12.0 crore credit cards growing at 8.5% a year. Private banks hold 70.9% of all credit cards, while public sector banks hold only 23.8%. Public banks control about 64% of debit cards, which means they already have millions of customers who could be offered credit cards at much lower cost than finding completely new customers.
a6c393217b7740b0.implication: Public sector banks should offer credit cards to their existing debit card customers, because they already know these people and trust them enough to give them debit cards, so the cost of getting a new credit card customer is very low.
chain: Private banks have 70.9% of credit cards but public banks have most of the debit cards in the country
Public banks already have a relationship with these debit card holders and know their banking behavior
Public banks can offer credit cards to these existing customers at very low cost compared to finding brand new customers

afa8ec7a9b2343af.body: India has 13.6 lakh micro ATMs that let villagers withdraw cash without visiting a full branch, but the number fell -8.1% recently. These machines are closing or fewer are being added even though people in small towns still need cash every day. A micro ATM costs far less to run than opening a real branch.
afa8ec7a9b2343af.implication: A bank should keep or add micro ATMs in villages where branches are too expensive, because villagers still need cash and these machines are cheap to operate.
chain: The count of micro ATMs dropped -8.1% so fewer machines are available in villages
Villagers still need cash daily but full branches cost too much to build and staff
Banks can serve these customers cheaply by keeping micro ATMs running instead of closing them

dd55acdd01924a45.body: Credit card spending in the 'other' category jumped 2366.0% in value and 714.0% in volume year-on-year. Millions of people are now tapping cards at metro gates, vending machines, and small shops that just installed tap-to-pay terminals. This is not existing cardholders spending more — it is people using cards in completely new places for the first time.
dd55acdd01924a45.implication: Banks should issue cards to people who ride the metro or shop at small stores, because these customers will start using cards for everyday purchases once the terminals are in place.
chain: Metro gates and small shops install tap-to-pay terminals
People who never used cards before start tapping to pay for rides and snacks
These new users keep the card in their wallet and begin using it for other purchases too
